paper_a.title: An Improved Data Stream Summary: The Count-Min Sketch and its Applications (Cormode & Muthukrishnan, 2003)

paper_b.title: Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors (Bloom, 1970)

metadata.description: Both papers design compact randomized data structures that hash items into a small array using k hash functions to answer approximate-membership-style queries with controlled false-positive rate. Bloom (1970) introduces the bit-array filter for Boolean set membership; Cormode-Muthukrishnan (2003) generalize the same hashing skeleton to a 2-D counter array supporting weighted point/range/inner-product/heavy-hitter/quantile queries on streaming frequency vectors. NOTE on labels: the registry swapped these two papers, so paper_a (paper311) is in fact the Count-Min Sketch paper and paper_b (paper312) is the Bloom Filter paper, the inverse of what the alignment_name 'BloomFilter_vs_CountMinSketch' suggests. Both inputs are PDF-fallback extractions, so we lean on names/types and treat exact-LaTeX matches loosely. We classify the relation as CF (competing frameworks) rather than EXT because Count-Min was developed for a different problem (frequency estimation in turnstile streams) with different analysis machinery (pairwise-independent hashing + Markov + median-of-means / Chernoff), even though it can be viewed in hindsight as a weighted generalization of Bloom's bit array.

matches.explanation: The Count-Min sketch (paper_a's central data structure: a d-by-w counter array with d pairwise-independent hash functions) is the direct weighted generalization of Bloom's Method 2 (paper_b's central data structure: an N''-bit array with d hash functions, each insertion setting d bits to 1). Both reserve a small array, hash each item to k cells, and aggregate per cell. CM stores integer counters and aggregates by addition; Bloom stores single bits and aggregates by OR. Type mismatch (definition vs. algorithm) reflects extraction granularity: Bloom's paper bundles 'data structure + insert/query' into one algorithm node, whereas CM splits the data structure (DP311.5) from update (AP311.1) and query (AP311.2/3) algorithms.

CM update procedure ('add c_t to cell count[j, h_j(i_t)] for each row j') is the weighted analogue of Bloom Method 2's insertion ('for i=1..d: bits[hash_i(m)] <- 1'). Both write to one cell per hash function; the only difference is +c_t vs. set-to-1. Cross-reference: AP312.2 also matches DP311.5 above on the data-structure side; here we align it on the insertion side because Bloom's algorithm node bundles both.

CM's non-negative point query (return min_j count[j, h_j(i)]) is the weighted analogue of Bloom Method 2's lookup (return 'reject' iff any of the d hashed bits is 0, else 'accept'). Bloom's lookup is a Boolean min-over-bits (AND); CM's lookup is an integer min-over-counters. Same skeleton, different semiring.

CM's general (signed) point query takes the median rather than the min of the d row estimates so as to handle negative entries. Bloom (1970) addresses only Boolean set membership and has no analogue of negative updates or median aggregation.

Both characterize the false-positive behavior of the structure. CM Theorem 1 bounds Pr[hat a_i > a_i + epsilon ||a||_1] <= delta for non-negative inputs via pairwise independence + Markov over d rows; Bloom's EP312.4 gives the closed-form false-positive probability P'' = (1 - phi'')^d for a Bloom filter. Both are the probabilistic guarantees on the basic (non-negative / Boolean) point query, and both decay exponentially in the number of hash functions d. Differs in object: CM gives a high-probability additive-error tail bound; Bloom gives the exact expected false-positive rate.

Both proofs analyze the failure probability of a hash-array membership-style structure with d hash functions. CM PP311.1 introduces collision indicators I_{i,j,k}, bounds E[X_{i,j}] <= (epsilon/e)||a||_1 by pairwise independence, then applies Markov across the d rows. Bloom PP312.2 computes the per-bit zero-probability phi'' = (1 - d/N'')^n by independence, then raises to the d-th power. The skeletons (per-hash-function probability under independence -> combine across the d hash functions) are parallel, but CM uses Markov's inequality and a min-aggregator while Bloom multiplies independent bit probabilities directly.

Composite L2 alignment under the parent proof match (PP311.1 <-> PP312.2). Both step DAGs follow 'introduce per-hash-function variable -> bound its expectation/probability -> combine over d hash functions': CM defines I_{i,j,k}, bounds E[X_{i,j}], then Markov-unions over j; Bloom defines phi'' = (1 - d/N'')^n, computes T'' = 1/phi'', then composes via P'' = (1 - phi'')^d. The arithmetic differs (additive Markov vs. multiplicative independence) but the step roles align.

CM Theorem 2 (signed-input median estimator with two-sided 3*epsilon*||a||_1 error bound via Chernoff over d rows) has no Bloom analogue; Bloom's Boolean filter has no median, no Chernoff, and no two-sided guarantee.
Proof of CM Theorem 2 (Chernoff over the median of d copies). Bloom has no analogue.
CM Theorem 3 bounds the inner-product estimator a-dot-b. Bloom does not consider inner products or weighted aggregates between two sets.
Proof of CM inner-product bound (per-row diagonal+collision decomposition + Markov). No Bloom analogue.
CM Corollary 1 (database join-size estimation via inner-product sketches). No Bloom analogue: Bloom's filter does not estimate aggregate quantities between two sets.
CM inner-product estimation algorithm. No Bloom analogue.
CM Theorem 4 (range query over dyadic decomposition with O(log n) sketches). Bloom has no range-query primitive.
Proof of CM range-query bound. No Bloom analogue.
CM range-query algorithm via dyadic decomposition. No Bloom analogue.
Definition of dyadic ranges, used only for CM range-query support. Bloom does not have a range concept.
CM Theorem 5: epsilon-approximate phi-quantiles in the turnstile model. Quantiles are absent from Bloom.
CM quantiles algorithm in the turnstile model. No Bloom analogue.
Definition of phi-quantiles. Bloom does not consider rank-based queries.
Quantile-finding problem on data streams. No Bloom analogue.
CM Theorem 6: heavy hitters in the cash-register model. Bloom is set-valued and does not output 'frequent items'.
Proof of CM heavy hitters (cash register). No Bloom analogue.
CM heavy hitters algorithm in the cash-register model. No Bloom analogue.
CM Theorem 7: heavy hitters in turnstile model via parallel binary search over O(log n) sketches. No Bloom analogue.
CM heavy-hitters algorithm in turnstile model. No Bloom analogue.

Problem-level kinship: both target an approximate-membership-style query on a large set / stream with a tunable false-positive parameter. Bloom's ProbP312.1 (hash-coded set membership with allowable errors) is the Boolean root problem; CM's ProbP311.2 (approximate phi-heavy hitters with epsilon slack) is a weighted generalization where membership is replaced by 'count exceeds a threshold'. Tagged 'low' because the problems differ in input model (static set vs. stream) and output (Boolean vs. ranked items).
Hierarchical heavy hitters problem. No Bloom analogue.

CM's open problem: design extremely simple, practical sketches like CM for estimating stream correlations and other complex aggregates. Bloom's paper, predating the streaming literature by three decades, has no open-problem nodes and no analogous research direction.
Turnstile / cash-register data-stream model. Bloom predates streaming and works with a static fixed set M of n messages.

Definition of CM point query Q(i) returning an approximation of a_i. The closest Bloom analogue is membership testing (ProbP312.1) rather than a numerical estimate; we route the cross-paper signal through that problem-level match instead, leaving DP311.2 unmatched as a CM-specific weighted query primitive.
Range-query definition. No Bloom analogue.
Inner-product query definition. No Bloom analogue.
Definition of phi-heavy hitters. No Bloom analogue.
Bloom's conventional (error-free) open-addressing hash table baseline. No CM counterpart: CM does not analyze or compare against an exact open-addressing baseline.
Bloom's Method 1 (small-cell open-addressing with c-bit codes per cell). No CM counterpart: CM does not use open-addressing or store truncated key codes.

Bloom's allowable-error fraction P (false-positive rate). CM uses (epsilon, delta) where epsilon parametrizes additive error magnitude and delta parametrizes failure probability; this is a different formal object than a single false-positive rate over a fixed message space.

Bloom's space factor N (bits in hash area). CM measures space as O((1/epsilon) log(1/delta)) words; the underlying notion is similar (memory footprint) but neither paper has an explicit definitional node that aligns at the same granularity, so we leave this unmatched.
Bloom's normalized reject-time T. CM does not analyze per-query bit-test counts and has no time analogue at this granularity.
Bloom's normalized space measure S = N / (-n log_2 P). CM does not normalize space against an information-theoretic lower bound.
Empty-cell fraction phi for the conventional open-addressing baseline. CM uses no open-addressing and has no empty-cell fraction concept.
Empty-cell fraction phi' for Bloom Method 1. No CM analogue.

Bloom's zero-bit fraction phi'' = (1 - d/N'')^n governs the bit-array's load. CM has a related per-row collision quantity (used inside PSP311.1-2 as 1/w) but it is not lifted to a definition node, and CM's combination rule is min over rows rather than (1-phi'')^d.
Bloom's conventional (error-free) space/time trade-off equation. CM has no error-free baseline and no space-vs-reject-time equation.
Bloom's Method 1 false-positive expression P' = (1/2)^{c-1}/phi'. CM has no Method-1-style analogue (it uses counter arrays, not c-bit code cells).
Bloom Method 1 three-factor (N', T', P') trade-off. No CM analogue.

Bloom Method 2 three-factor trade-off N'' = n(-log_2 P'') log_2 e / (log_2(1/T'') log_2(1 - 1/T'')). CM proves a space bound O((1/epsilon) ln(1/delta)) (in TP311.1 / RP311.1) that plays the same role -- 'space as a function of error parameters' -- but it is integrated into the theorem statements and the b=e remark rather than emitted as a standalone equation node, so a clean L1 alignment is not available.
Bloom's normalized-space curves S' and S'' for cross-method comparison. No CM analogue.

Bloom's Proposition: for fixed P'', S'' is minimized at phi''=1/2, i.e. T''=2, where S''=log_2 e ~ 1.47. CM's RP311.1 (the b=e remark) plays a parallel role: it identifies the optimal hash-base / per-row size that minimizes the space cost (2 + e/epsilon) ln(1/delta), with the optimum at b=e. Both are 'optimum tuning of the per-hash-function parameter to minimize space at fixed error', but they live in different parameter spaces (Boolean bit-array vs. counter array) and use different algebra. Tagged low because the formal objects are not equal and the alignment is best read as a conceptual/methodological echo.

Bloom proofs internal to Method 1 (PP312.1), the conventional baseline (PP312.0), and the optimum-at-T''=2 derivation (PP312.3). None of these targets has a CM counterpart: Method 1 and the conventional baseline are absent from CM, and CM's optimization of b is left as a one-line remark rather than a proved proposition.

Bloom's proposition that Method 2 dominates Method 1 in normalized space. No CM analogue: CM does not compare two of its own methods; the closest comparison is the cross-sketch survey (RP311.3) but that is qualitative.
